case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal limits on coordinated expenditures by political parties (as applied to plaintiffs) violate the First Amendment, or whether that challenge is foreclosed by Supreme Court precedent—especially FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II)—such that lower courts cannot reach the merits absent a change by the Supreme Court.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) coordinated party expenditure limits (i.e., statutory caps on party spending made in coordination with a candidate), challenged under the First Amendment (free speech and association).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Plaintiffs/petitioners argue that FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits unconstitutionally burden political speech and associational rights under the First Amendment. Although Colorado II rejected a facial challenge to these limits, plaintiffs contend their suit is materially different because (i) they bring an as-applied challenge and/or advance arguments not previously presented, and (ii) intervening doctrinal developments in campaign-finance and First Amendment law have undermined Colorado II’s reasoning—so lower courts should not treat Colorado II as controlling or should at least permit the challenge to proceed for higher-court reconsideration.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FEC/respondent argues that Colorado II directly controls because it upheld the constitutionality of coordinated party expenditure limits against a constitutional challenge grounded in the same core theory (that such limits violate the First Amendment). Under vertical stare decisis, inferior courts must follow directly applicable Supreme Court precedent even if later cases arguably weaken its reasoning. Accordingly, the plaintiffs’ effort to repackage a previously rejected facial challenge as an as-applied challenge—based on substantially the same factual and legal premises—cannot be decided on the merits by lower courts, and should be dismissed/denied (or, in FECA’s special review structure, not certified for en banc appellate review beyond the narrow threshold inquiry).
key_precedents: FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II), 533 U.S. 431 (2001)
Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/Am. Exp., Inc., 490 U.S. 477 (1989)
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022)
Thompson v. Marietta Education Ass’n, 972 F.3d 809 (6th Cir. 2020)
Limbach v. Hooven & Allison Co., 466 U.S. 353 (1984)
California Medical Ass’n v. FEC, 453 U.S. 182 (1981)
California Water Service Co. v. City of Redding, 304 U.S. 252 (1938)
Mariani v. United States, 212 F.3d 761 (3d Cir. 2000)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that coordinated party spending is core political speech and that later cases have tightened the definition of corruption, so the limits deserve renewed First Amendment scrutiny. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, Colorado II directly upheld these coordinated party-expenditure caps on the premise petitioners challenge—treating coordination as contribution-like and crediting anticircumvention interests—and Rodriguez de Quijas bars lower courts from treating doctrinal drift as an implied overruling. Labeling this challenge “as-applied” does not materially narrow it, because the application complained of is the ordinary operation of the very limits Colorado II sustained, not some distinct enforcement anomaly or uniquely low cap that precludes effective advocacy. Petitioners have standing to sue, but that only gets them in the courthouse door; it does not authorize a lower-court merits reconsideration that would effectively overrule controlling precedent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that this is styled as an as-applied challenge to concrete, intended coordinated expenditures, so Article III presents no obstacle and relief could, in theory, be tailored to them alone. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, the supposed narrowing does not meaningfully distinguish this case from Colorado II’s holding upholding these very coordinated party-expenditure limits; accepting petitioners’ theory would invite lower courts to treat Colorado II as functionally overruled. That sort of "as-applied" label cannot be used to obtain relief that, as a practical matter, disables the statute’s ordinary operation—something inconsistent with remedial restraint and the limits of the judicial role. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, any reconsideration of Colorado II is for this Court, not to be accomplished by indirection in inferior courts on a record that does not identify a genuinely distinct application.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point is that these caps burden core political speech and association and that later cases may have narrowed the permissible anticorruption rationale, but that goes to whether Colorado II should be reconsidered, not whether lower courts may disregard it. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Colorado II squarely upheld these coordinated party-expenditure limits on the coordination-as-contribution and anticircumvention theory, and Rodriguez de Quijas forecloses treating doctrinal “drift” as an implied overruling. The “as-applied” label does not meaningfully narrow the claim because it targets the statute’s ordinary operation rather than a genuinely distinct application supported by concrete, application-specific facts that would take this case outside Colorado II. On this posture and record, it would be premature to reweigh Congress’s anticircumvention judgment or to undertake an effective overruling by indirection; any such reconsideration must come from this Court with a candid stare decisis analysis and a fully developed record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest contention—that these caps burden core party speech and association and thus merit renewed, more searching First Amendment review—runs into Colorado II’s controlling classification of coordinated party expenditures as contribution-like. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, labeling this challenge “as-applied” does not supply application-specific facts or objective evidence of a distinct, heightened burden that would take it outside Colorado II’s holding; it instead seeks to relitigate the same theory on a thin record. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts cannot treat alleged doctrinal drift as permission to disregard directly controlling precedent, and absent a concrete evidentiary showing of exceptional burden, facial-like invalidation by indirection is unwarranted. The longstanding anticircumvention rationale for regulating coordination therefore remains sufficient at this posture, and the judgment should be for the FEC.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that coordinated party spending can look like core party speech and association, and that later cases have tightened the corruption interest—so perhaps Colorado II’s anticircumvention rationale deserves reexamination. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the question at this posture is not whether Colorado II was rightly decided under today’s campaign-finance doctrine; it is whether inferior courts may treat alleged doctrinal drift as permission to disregard a decision that directly controls. Colorado II already did the essential characterization work—coordination converts party spending into a candidate-centered value transfer, contribution-like in its mechanism and thus governed by Buckley’s more deferential framework—so petitioners’ “as-applied” label does not supply a materially distinct application or the “rare case” of a limit so low it precludes effective advocacy. Any reconsideration must be candidly undertaken by this Court in a proper stare decisis analysis, not accomplished by indirection through an as-applied challenge that targets the statute’s ordinary operation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ best argument is that this is an as-applied First Amendment challenge and that later cases have narrowed what counts as “corruption,” inviting fresh scrutiny of coordinated party spending. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, what petitioners call “as-applied” is just the statute’s ordinary operation—precisely the coordinated party-expenditure caps Colorado II upheld on anticorruption and anticircumvention grounds. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts may not treat doctrinal drift as a license to disregard a directly controlling decision; whatever the merits of revisiting Colorado II, that is this Court’s work, not the inferior courts’. Given that posture, and mindful of remedial modesty, the correct course is to affirm for the FEC rather than effectively overrule Colorado II by indirection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that subsequent campaign-finance decisions have narrowed permissible anticorruption rationales and arguably elevated parties’ First Amendment status, suggesting Colorado II’s reasoning has weakened. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, vertical stare decisis under Rodriguez de Quijas requires lower courts to follow Colorado II because it directly upheld these coordinated party-expenditure limits on the coordination-as-contribution and anticircumvention theories. The “as-applied” label does not materially distinguish this case: petitioners challenge the ordinary operation of the very caps Colorado II sustained, not a genuinely application-specific anomaly such as a uniquely low limit that forecloses effective advocacy. Any reconsideration of Colorado II must be squarely sought in this Court with full briefing and traditional stare decisis analysis, not accomplished by indirection.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioners’ best move is to repackage their claim as “as-applied,” insisting that the burdens here turn on application-specific facts and thus fall outside Colorado II. But as the Chief Justice notes, that label does not materially narrow the legal theory: the alleged injury arises from the ordinary operation of the coordinated party-expenditure caps that Colorado II upheld by treating coordination as contribution-like and crediting anticircumvention interests. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts must follow that directly controlling holding notwithstanding later doctrinal “drift,” and petitioners have not identified a distinct factual posture (e.g., a uniquely low cap or atypical enforcement feature) that would allow relief without functionally overruling Colorado II by indirection. The proper course at this posture is therefore to enforce Colorado II and resolve the case for the FEC, leaving any reconsideration of that precedent to this Court on a squarely presented request.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest contention is that intervening campaign-finance cases have narrowed the corruption rationale and heightened skepticism of spending limits, so coordinated party spending should now be treated more like independent expenditures. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan underscore, that is fundamentally a request to revisit Colorado II, not a basis for a lower court to disregard it: under Rodriguez de Quijas, doctrinal “drift” cannot be transmuted into an as-applied carveout when the application challenged is the ordinary operation Colorado II already upheld. Framed properly, petitioners have not identified a materially distinct factual posture (e.g., a coordination regime meaningfully different from the one Colorado II assessed, or a record showing a limit so low it forecloses effective advocacy) that would trigger a different First Amendment framework rather than Colorado II’s contribution-like/anticircumvention analysis. Given this posture and the plaintiffs’ burden, vertical stare decisis forecloses merits re-litigation in the lower courts absent an intervening decision that actually displaces Colorado II.

John Roberts.reasoning: The plaintiffs identify a concrete injury to core campaign speech and associational activity—being subject to statutory caps and penalties that deter coordinated party expenditures—and that injury is fairly traceable to FECA and redressable by an injunction, so Article III standing is satisfied. On the merits, however, Colorado II upheld these same coordinated party expenditure limits on the rationale that coordination with a candidate makes the spending functionally equivalent to a contribution and that limits are justified to prevent circumvention of contribution caps; that holding squarely addresses the constitutional question the plaintiffs press, notwithstanding their effort to label it “as-applied.” Under vertical stare decisis, lower courts (and thus this posture) must follow directly controlling Supreme Court precedent even if later cases arguably cast doubt on its reasoning; only this Court may overrule Colorado II. Because the challenge is foreclosed absent a decision to revisit Colorado II, the proper disposition is to rule for the FEC rather than reach the First Amendment merits anew.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III permits federal courts to resolve only the concrete dispute before them, and the proper course is to tailor any relief—if warranted—to the plaintiffs’ specific intended coordinated expenditures rather than pronounce a broad rule disabling FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits. But here the plaintiffs’ “as-applied” framing does not meaningfully narrow the claim; it asks lower courts to revisit the same constitutional theory Colorado II upheld as to coordinated party spending, which would require treating that precedent as effectively overruled. Under vertical stare decisis, inferior courts must follow directly controlling Supreme Court decisions even if later cases arguably undermine their reasoning, leaving any reconsideration of Colorado II to this Court. Accordingly, the challenge is foreclosed in the lower courts and should be denied/dismissed at that stage rather than entertained on the merits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The dispositive threshold issue is posture: plaintiffs seek to relitigate FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure caps notwithstanding Colorado II, which upheld these limits by treating coordinated spending as functionally equivalent to contributions and sustaining the regime against a First Amendment attack. Under vertical stare decisis, lower courts may not disregard directly controlling Supreme Court precedent on the ground that later cases arguably erode its reasoning; that is for this Court alone to reconsider, so the merits cannot be reached absent a genuine, materially distinct as-applied record. On the limited showing described, plaintiffs have not identified application-specific facts demonstrating that their situation falls outside Colorado II’s holding (as opposed to recharacterizing the same coordinated activity), and a court should not engage in “premature” re-interpretation of FECA on an undeveloped record. Accordingly, the challenge is foreclosed at this stage, and any request to overrule or narrow Colorado II must be addressed by this Court, not a lower tribunal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The regulation at issue is not a disclosure regime with indirect, modest burdens; it is a limit on coordinated party expenditures that Colorado II specifically classified as the functional equivalent of contributions, and the Court has long treated contribution limits as permissible under a more deferential, means–end fit inquiry aimed at preventing quid pro quo corruption and circumvention. Under vertical stare decisis, lower courts are foreclosed from reaching the merits where Supreme Court precedent “directly controls,” even if petitioners argue intervening doctrinal drift, because it is this Court’s prerogative—not an inferior court’s—to overrule or narrow Colorado II. Petitioners’ attempt to recast a previously rejected theory as “as-applied” fails absent a materially distinct factual record showing a different kind or magnitude of First Amendment burden than Colorado II addressed; nothing here demonstrates an objective, case-specific burden that would take their claim outside Colorado II’s holding. Given the settled practice of regulating coordinated expenditures as contributions and the absence of a genuinely new, evidentiary basis for distinguishing this application, the challenge is foreclosed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Buckley’s settled framework, coordinated party expenditures have been treated as the functional equivalent of contributions because coordination creates the same candidate-centered value transfer and corresponding quid pro quo risk that justifies contribution limits; Colorado II applied that principle to uphold FECA’s coordinated party expenditure caps as a contribution-type regulation subject to more deferential review. Plaintiffs’ effort to relabel the claim as “as-applied” does not change the law’s object or mechanism (a cap on party spending made in coordination with a candidate), nor do they show the ‘rare case’ where the limit is so low as to preclude effective advocacy, given that parties remain free to make substantial coordinated spending up to the cap and unlimited independent expenditures. And as a matter of vertical stare decisis, lower courts may not treat later doctrinal shifts as license to disregard a directly controlling Supreme Court holding; any reconsideration of Colorado II’s anti-corruption judgment and contribution-equivalence rule is for this Court alone.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure caps undeniably regulate political expression and association, and any such restriction must be justified by at least a significant governmental interest—and, if content based, strict scrutiny. But at this procedural posture the dispositive question is not whether the limits survive scrutiny in the abstract; it is whether inferior courts may revisit that merits question when this Court has already upheld these very coordinated-party limits in Colorado II on an anticorruption (and circumvention) rationale. Under vertical stare decisis, lower courts must follow directly controlling Supreme Court precedent even if later decisions have arguably eroded its reasoning, so plaintiffs’ re-labeling of substantially the same theory as “as applied” does not free the lower court to reach the merits. The appropriate course is to enforce Colorado II unless and until this Court changes course, rather than for a lower court to effectively overrule it by indirection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The plaintiffs’ First Amendment claim targets FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits, but Colorado II squarely upheld those limits against a constitutional challenge premised on the same core theory that coordinated party spending may be restricted to prevent corruption and its appearance. Under vertical stare decisis and Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts must follow directly applicable Supreme Court precedent even if later campaign-finance decisions arguably undermine its reasoning; any request to depart from or overrule Colorado II must be made to, and addressed by, this Court with full briefing and traditional stare decisis analysis. Labeling the claim “as-applied” does not allow a lower court to reach the merits when the application here is the ordinary operation of the very coordinated-expenditure caps Colorado II sustained. Accordingly, the challenge is foreclosed in the lower courts absent a change by the Supreme Court.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The threshold question is not whether petitioners can articulate a plausible First Amendment theory, but whether any lower court may reach that merits question in light of controlling Supreme Court precedent. Colorado II upheld FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits against a First Amendment challenge, rejecting the proposition that such coordinated party spending must be treated like independent expenditures, and that holding squarely covers the core theory petitioners press even if they label it “as-applied.” Under Rodriguez de Quijas, doctrinal drift in later campaign-finance cases does not authorize inferior courts to disregard a directly applicable Supreme Court decision unless this Court has plainly abandoned it; petitioners’ asserted factual distinctions about their particular coordination do not identify a materially different legal rule or a narrowed application outside Colorado II’s sweep. On this record, vertical stare decisis forecloses merits reconsideration in the lower courts, so judgment should be for the FEC absent a change by this Court.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The threshold question here is not the ultimate First Amendment merits but the proper doctrinal framework for an inferior court confronting a challenge to FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits: vertical stare decisis. Colorado II specifically upheld those coordinated party limits against a First Amendment attack premised on the constitutional significance of party–candidate coordination and the Government’s anticircumvention/anticorruption interests, and plaintiffs’ effort to relabel the claim as “as-applied” does not materially change the controlling factual predicate (party spending coordinated with a candidate) or the governing legal rule. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts must follow directly applicable Supreme Court precedent even if subsequent developments arguably undermine its reasoning; only this Court may decide whether Colorado II should be revisited. Given plaintiffs’ burden—especially to the extent they seek sweeping relief that functions like a facial invalidation—the record and posture do not permit a lower court to disregard Colorado II and reach the merits absent an intervening decision that actually displaces it.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether lower federal courts may entertain and potentially uphold an as-applied (or renewed facial) First Amendment challenge to FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits when the Supreme Court in Colorado II already rejected materially the same constitutional attack, absent intervening Supreme Court developments that clearly displace Colorado II.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) provisions limiting ‘coordinated’ expenditures by political parties in connection with federal candidates (i.e., coordinated party expenditure limits), challenged under the First Amendment (speech and association).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Plaintiffs/petitioners argue that FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits unconstitutionally burden political parties’ and speakers’ First Amendment rights. They contend Colorado II should not control because the doctrinal landscape has changed (post-Colorado II campaign-finance cases allegedly undermining its reasoning), and because they offer new legal and factual arguments supporting heightened skepticism of coordinated-spending caps. They frame their suit to have at least ‘arguable merit’ warranting review (including under FECA’s special certification/en banc review structure), even if it asks for Colorado II to be revisited or limited.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FEC/respondent argues that Colorado II directly forecloses the challenge because it upheld the constitutionality of coordinated party-expenditure limits against a facial First Amendment attack, expressly recognizing the anti-circumvention rationale (coordinated spending can function like a contribution). Under vertical stare decisis, lower courts must follow on-point Supreme Court precedent (Rodriguez de Quijas), and cannot reach the merits to effectively overrule Colorado II. The FEC also presses procedural/structural points under FECA’s review scheme: district courts should not engage in broad ‘legislative fact’ finding or merits-like re-litigation inconsistent with the statute’s allocation of responsibilities to the court of appeals (en banc) and the Supreme Court.

Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/Am. Express, Inc., 490 U.S. 477 (1989)
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022)
Limbach v. Hooven & Allison Co., 466 U.S. (1984)
Thompson v. Marietta Education Ass’n, 972 F.3d 809 (6th Cir. 2020)
California Medical Ass’n v. FEC, 453 U.S. 182 (1981)
California Water Service Co. v. City of Redding, 304 U.S. 252 (1938)
Mariani v. United States, 212 F.3d 761 (3d Cir. 2000)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point is that our post-Colorado II cases have narrowed the anticorruption interest to quid pro quo and rejected broader “influence/access” rationales, arguably weakening Colorado II’s anticircumvention analysis. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, whatever doctrinal tension exists does not make intervening decisions clearly irreconcilable with Colorado II’s core holding that coordination renders spending the functional equivalent of a contribution, and Rodriguez de Quijas bars lower courts from treating directly controlling precedent as implicitly overruled. I also agree with Justice Sotomayor that the “as-applied” label here does not rest on a materially distinct, plaintiff-specific record; on this posture it operates as a renewed facial attack seeking to relitigate Colorado II wholesale. The appropriate disposition is therefore to apply Colorado II and reject the invitation for inferior courts to nullify it indirectly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that our later campaign-finance decisions have narrowed the anticorruption interest to quid pro quo, supposedly leaving Colorado II’s anticircumvention rationale without constitutional footing. But as the Chief Justice explains, whatever tension exists in rationale, Colorado II’s holding—coordination makes party spending functionally contribution-like—remains directly controlling, and Rodriguez de Quijas bars lower courts from treating it as implicitly overruled. I also agree with Justice Sotomayor that petitioners’ “as-applied” framing seeks relief untethered to a concrete, plaintiff-specific application and record, effectively inviting an advisory facial pronouncement beyond Article III’s proper limits. On this posture, the renewed constitutional attack should be rejected unless and until this Court revisits Colorado II on an appropriate record with relief cabined to proven injury.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest counterargument is that post-Colorado II campaign-finance cases have narrowed the corruption interest to quid pro quo, purportedly leaving Colorado II’s anti-circumvention rationale without footing. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, those later decisions do not “entirely displace” Colorado II’s controlling holding that coordinated party expenditures may be treated as contribution-like precisely because coordination enables circumvention of contribution limits—an interest still recognized even under a quid-pro-quo framework. On this record, petitioners’ effort is essentially a renewed facial attack (or a relabeled as-applied challenge) seeking broad relief untethered to materially distinct facts, and Rodriguez de Quijas forbids lower courts from anticipating this Court’s overruling of directly controlling precedent. Absent a genuinely different application supported by a developed factual record, the challenge is foreclosed and should be rejected.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest petitioner-side contention would be that intervening campaign-finance cases have so narrowed the anticorruption interest that Colorado II’s anti-circumvention rationale is no longer viable, but that is not enough for an inferior court to disregard directly controlling precedent. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Rodriguez de Quijas requires lower courts to apply Colorado II unless an intervening decision clearly and irreconcilably displaces its holding, and petitioners show at most doctrinal tension. Nor have petitioners supplied an objective, record-based showing of a materially different, substantial First Amendment burden—i.e., evidence of actual chilling, threats, or a distinct application outside Colorado II’s plainly legitimate sweep—such that this is genuinely “as-applied” rather than a relabeled facial challenge. Respect for precedent and the limits of facial adjudication counsel rejecting an invitation to reopen Colorado II on a thin or speculative record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that our later cases narrowed the anticorruption interest to quid pro quo, supposedly draining Colorado II’s anticircumvention rationale. But as the Chief Justice (and Justice Kavanaugh) explains, whatever doctrinal tension exists, those later decisions have not clearly and irreconcilably displaced Colorado II’s holding that coordination makes party spending contribution-like and thus regulable; under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts must follow that on-point precedent rather than treat it as implicitly overruled. And as Justice Sotomayor underscores, labeling this suit “as-applied” does not supply a materially distinct application or record—petitioners seek broad relief that functions facially, without the required accounting of constitutional versus unconstitutional applications. On this posture, the lower courts cannot relitigate Colorado II’s merits in a way that effectively nullifies it; only we can revisit that precedent, and this case is not presented in a posture that justifies doing so.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that our post-Colorado II cases have tightened the anticorruption interest to quid pro quo, purportedly draining Colorado II’s anti-circumvention rationale. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, that is an overruling argument, and Rodriguez de Quijas forbids lower courts from treating directly controlling precedent as implicitly displaced absent a clearly irreconcilable intervening holding. Nor does the “as-applied” label do any real work here: without a materially distinct application and plaintiff-specific record, the relief sought functions facially and cannot satisfy the demanding Stevens/Washington State Grange standards for invalidation. If a future case presents a concrete, atypical application outside Colorado II’s legitimate sweep, any remedy should be narrowly tailored to the plaintiffs’ proven injury rather than rewriting FECA wholesale.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that our later campaign-finance cases narrowed the anticorruption interest to quid pro quo corruption and cast doubt on broader “influence/access” rationales. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, that is at most an argument for this Court to reconsider Colorado II—not a basis for lower courts to treat it as implicitly overruled—because Colorado II’s holding squarely rests on the doctrinal rule that coordination makes party spending contribution-like and regulable to prevent circumvention. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, doctrinal tension is not “clearly irreconcilable” displacement, and administrability strongly counsels against inviting inferior courts to decide when precedent has been sufficiently “undermined” to ignore. Relabeling the claim as “as-applied” does not materially change the legal question where the same provision and the same asserted constitutional defect are being pressed for effectively facial relief, as Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor note.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that our post-Colorado II cases have tightened the corruption interest to quid pro quo, arguably weakening Colorado II’s anticircumvention rationale. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explained, that is an overruling argument, and under Rodriguez de Quijas lower courts may not treat doctrinal tension as license to disregard a precedent that directly controls the same provision and theory—coordination makes party spending contribution-like and therefore regulable. Nor does the “as-applied” label solve the problem here; absent a materially distinct application and record-based showing of burden, the requested relief functions facially and would effectively nullify Colorado II. If Colorado II is to be revisited, it must be by this Court on a posture that genuinely presents a distinct application rather than inviting lower courts to anticipate our overrulings.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that our post–Colorado II cases have tightened the anticorruption interest toward quid pro quo, allegedly draining Colorado II’s anticircumvention rationale. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, whatever doctrinal tension exists, Rodriguez de Quijas requires lower courts to apply directly controlling precedent unless a later decision is clearly irreconcilable with it—and none of the intervening cases expressly repudiates Colorado II’s coordination-as-contribution holding. Nor does petitioners’ relabeling as “as-applied,” emphasized by Justice Sotomayor, supply a materially distinct factual posture or developed record that would permit narrower, posture-sensitive First Amendment adjudication rather than a de facto facial overruling. In this posture, the high bar for broad First Amendment invalidation is not met, and the lower courts must adhere to Colorado II unless and until this Court revisits it.

John Roberts.reasoning: As a threshold matter, assuming plaintiffs can show a concrete, imminent chill from threatened enforcement of FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits that is fairly traceable to the FEC and redressable by an injunction, the dispositive problem is not justiciability but vertical stare decisis. Colorado II upheld these coordinated party-expenditure limits against a materially identical First Amendment facial challenge on the ground that coordinated spending may be treated like a contribution and thus regulated to prevent quid pro quo corruption and circumvention, and under Rodriguez de Quijas lower courts may not entertain the merits to effectively overrule that directly controlling decision. Post-Colorado II cases tightening the anticorruption rationale to quid pro quo and rejecting “influence or access” do not “entirely displace” Colorado II’s core holding that coordination converts spending into the functional equivalent of a contribution, so inferior courts must apply Colorado II unless and until this Court revisits it. Where the line is close, our First Amendment tradition favors protecting political speech, but that principle does not authorize lower courts to disregard controlling precedent on the same restriction and the same anticircumvention rationale.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III permits us to decide only a concrete dispute as applied to the parties, and lower courts likewise may not issue what amounts to an advisory pronouncement that a statute is unconstitutional in hypothetical applications. Here, Colorado II already rejected a materially identical First Amendment facial attack on FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits, so an inferior court’s entertaining a renewed facial challenge (or an as-applied challenge that merely repackages the same theory without a distinct plaintiff-specific injury and record) would exceed traditional remedial limits and disregard vertical stare decisis. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts must follow directly controlling Supreme Court precedent even if later cases arguably cast doubt on its reasoning; only this Court may overrule Colorado II, and absent a clearly irreconcilable intervening decision, Colorado II remains binding. Because petitioners’ theory depends on displacing Colorado II rather than demonstrating a genuinely narrower, plaintiff-specific unconstitutional application, the challenge should be rejected on that basis.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Colorado II already addressed and rejected a facial First Amendment attack on FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits on the theory that coordinated spending can function like a contribution and may be limited to prevent circumvention; that holding has direct application here. Under Article III limits and my consistent skepticism of facial (or facial-like) challenges, lower courts should not entertain a re-litigation that effectively seeks broad relief untethered to a concrete, materially distinct record—especially where the challenge is, in substance, a request to overrule controlling precedent. Rodriguez de Quijas makes clear that absent intervening Supreme Court developments that clearly displace Colorado II, lower courts must follow the case that “directly controls,” rather than anticipate overruling based on perceived doctrinal trends. Because petitioners have not shown a genuinely different as-applied posture or a record establishing a constitutionally relevant distinction, the challenge is foreclosed and should be rejected.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado II squarely upheld FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits against a facial First Amendment challenge on the ground that coordinated party spending can operate like a contribution and thus may be limited to prevent circumvention; under vertical stare decisis, lower courts must apply that holding unless and until this Court clearly overrules it. Petitioners’ attempt to relitigate the same constitutional theory by recasting it as an as-applied (or renewed facial) challenge does not supply the objective, record-based showing of a materially different, substantial burden on a substantial proportion of affected parties necessary to justify departing from settled precedent. Nor do they identify intervening Supreme Court decisions that “entirely displaced” Colorado II’s governing rule in a way that would permit an inferior court to treat it as abandoned; at most they argue tensions in reasoning, which Rodriguez de Quijas instructs lower courts to leave for this Court. Respect for precedent and institutional restraint therefore require adherence to Colorado II and rejection of efforts to reopen the merits in the lower courts absent a genuinely new factual record demonstrating concrete First Amendment harm.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The first step is to get the posture right: Colorado II already rejected a facial First Amendment attack on these same coordinated party-expenditure limits, and plaintiffs’ repackaging as an as-applied (or “renewed” facial) challenge cannot license a lower court to relitigate the same constitutional theory on essentially the same statute absent a genuinely new application or materially different facts. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, when a Supreme Court precedent directly controls, lower courts must follow it even if later cases arguably cast doubt on its reasoning; only this Court may decide whether Colorado II should be overruled, and the asserted “doctrinal drift” in campaign-finance law is not the kind of clear displacement that makes Colorado II inoperative. Nor does the plaintiffs’ argument supply the kind of mapping of applications that could satisfy First Amendment facial review: Colorado II identified a substantial “plainly legitimate sweep” grounded in anti-circumvention (coordinated spending functioning contribution-like), and nothing here shows unconstitutional applications substantial in relation to that sweep. So the lower courts may not entertain the merits in a way that effectively nullifies Colorado II’s controlling holding; the challenge is foreclosed unless and until this Court revisits that precedent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Colorado II already rejected a materially identical First Amendment facial attack on FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure limits, and under vertical stare decisis lower courts must follow directly on-point Supreme Court precedent even if later cases cast doubt on its reasoning. Petitioners’ attempt to repackage the same constitutional claim as “as-applied” (or as a renewed facial challenge) cannot proceed absent a concrete, materially distinct factual posture showing the law’s operation differs from what Colorado II addressed, or an intervening Supreme Court decision that clearly displaces Colorado II’s holding rather than merely “undermining” it. On this record, the request amounts to asking inferior courts to anticipate overruling, which Rodriguez de Quijas forbids, and it also seeks broad relief untethered to plaintiff-specific facts—precisely the kind of facial, democracy-short-circuiting adjudication our precedents caution against. The proper course is to apply Colorado II unless and until this Court revisits it, and any remedy in the meantime must be confined to proven, plaintiff-specific injury rather than reopening the statute wholesale.
